response.text:
I looked at him, lost in astonishment. There he was before me, in motley, as though he had absconded from a troupe of mimes, enthusiastic, fabulous. His very existence was improbable, inexplicable. He said, with a flash of teeth in a bepatched face, that I must take Kurtz away quick—quick. The glamour of youth enveloped his parti-coloured rags and his destitution. He had lived for months, for years, with his life not worth a day’s purchase, and yet stood gallantly alive by the mere audacity of his few years. I was seduced into something like admiration. If the absolutely uncalculating spirit of adventure had ever ruled a being, it ruled this youth. I almost envied the clear flame that consumed all thought of self. But I did not envy him his devotion to Kurtz. He accepted it with eager fatalism. It seemed to me the most dangerous thing he had come upon.

They had come together unavoidably. I suppose Kurtz wanted an audience. One night, encamped in the forest, they had talked till dawn—more likely Kurtz had talked. “We talked of everything,” he said, transported. “Everything! Everything!... Of love, too.”

“Ah, he talked to you of love!” I said.

“It isn’t what you think,” he cried. “It was in general. He made me see things—things.”

He threw up his arms; the headman of my wood-cutters turned upon him heavy, glittering eyes. I assure you never before had this land, this river, this sky, appeared to me so hopeless and so dark, so impenetrable and pitiless. “And ever since, you have been with him?” I said.

On the contrary, their intercourse had been much broken. He had nursed Kurtz through two illnesses—“as you would to some risky feat”—but as a rule Kurtz wandered alone, far into the depths. “Very often, coming to this station, I had to wait days and days before he would turn up,” he said. “Ah, it was worth waiting for!—sometimes.”

“What was he doing? exploring or what?” I asked.

“Oh, yes, of course.” He had discovered lots of villages—a lake too—he did not know exactly in what direction. Mostly his expeditions were for ivory.

“But he had no goods to trade with by that time,” I objected.

“There’s a good lot of cartridges left even yet,” he said, looking away.

“To speak plainly, he raided the country,” I said.

He nodded.

“Not alone, surely!”

He muttered of villages around that lake.

“Kurtz got the tribe to follow him?” I suggested.

“They adored him,” he said. The mingled eagerness and reluctance with which he spoke of Kurtz were curious. “What can you expect?” he burst out; “he came to them with thunder and lightning—you know—and they had never seen anything like it. He could be very terrible. You can’t judge Mr. Kurtz as you would an ordinary man. No, no! Now just to give you an idea—I don’t mind telling you, he wanted to shoot me, too, one day—but I don’t judge him.”

“Shoot you!” I cried. “What for?”

“Well, I had a small lot of ivory the chief of that village near my house gave me. He wanted it, wouldn’t hear reason. Declared he would shoot me unless I gave him the ivory and then cleared out, because he could do so and had a fancy for it, and there was nothing on earth to prevent him killing whom he jolly well pleased. And it was true, too. I gave him the ivory. What did I care! But I didn’t clear out. No, no. I couldn’t leave him. I had to be careful, of course, till we got friendly again for a time. Afterwards I had to keep out of the way; but I didn’t mind. He was living for the most part in those villages on the lake. When he came down to the river, sometimes he would take to me, and sometimes it was better for me to be careful. This man suffered too much. He hated all this, and somehow he couldn’t get away. When I had a chance I begged him to try and leave while there was time; I offered to go back with him. And he would say yes, and then he would remain; go off on another ivory hunt; disappear for weeks; forget himself amongst these people—forget himself—you know.”

“Why! he’s mad,” I said.

He protested indignantly that Mr. Kurtz couldn’t be mad; had I heard him talk, only two days ago, I wouldn’t dare hint at such a thing.

I had taken up my binoculars and was looking at the shore, sweeping the forest’s limit at each side and at the back of the house. The consciousness of there being people in that bush, so silent, so quiet—as silent as the ruined house—made me uneasy. There was no sign on the face of nature of this amazing tale that was rather suggested to me in desolate exclamations, shrugs, hints ending in deep sighs. The woods were unmoved, like a mask—heavy, like a prison’s closed door—looking with their air of hidden knowledge and patient expectation.

It was only lately, the Russian said, that Kurtz had come down to the river, bringing with him all the fighting men of that lake tribe. He had been absent for several months—getting himself adored, I suppose—and had come down unexpectedly, with the intention of making a raid either across the river or down stream. Evidently the appetite for more ivory had got the better of the—what shall I say?—less material aspirations. However, he had got much worse suddenly. “I heard he was lying helpless, and so I came up—took my chance,” he said. “Oh, he is bad, very bad.”

I turned my glass to the house. No sign of life; the ruined roof, the long mud wall with three little square window-holes, no two the same size. Then one of the remaining posts of that vanished fence leaped up in my field. I had been struck at a distance by certain attempts at ornamentation; now I had a nearer view, and its first result was to make me throw my head back as if before a blow. These round knobs were not ornamental but symbolic; striking and disturbing—food for thought and also for such ants as were industrious enough to ascend the pole. They would have been even more impressive, those heads on the stakes, if their faces had not been turned to the house. Only one, the first I had made out, was facing my way. I returned to it deliberately—and there it was, black, dried, sunken, with closed eyelids—a head that seemed to sleep at the top of that pole; and, with the shrunken dry lips showing a narrow white line of the teeth, was smiling, too, at some endless and jocose dream of that eternal slumber.

I am not disclosing any trade secrets. The manager said afterwards that Mr. Kurtz’s methods had ruined the district. I want you to understand that there was nothing exactly profitable in these heads being there. They only showed that Mr. Kurtz lacked restraint in the gratification of his various lusts; that there was something wanting in him—some small matter which, when the pressing need arose, could not be found under his magnificent eloquence. Whether he knew of this deficiency I can’t say. I think the knowledge came to him at last—only at the very last. But the wilderness had found him out early, and had taken on him a terrible vengeance. I think it had whispered to him things about himself which he did not know; the whisper proved irresistibly fascinating. It echoed loudly within him because he was hollow at the core. I put down the glass, and the head that had appeared near enough to be spoken to leaped away into inaccessible distance.

His admirer was a bit crestfallen, and began to assure me in a hurried, indistinct voice that he had not dared to take these—say, symbols—down. He was not afraid of the natives; they would not stir till Mr. Kurtz gave the word. His ascendancy was extraordinary. The camps of these people surrounded the place, and the chiefs came every day to see him. They would crawl—

“I don’t want to know anything of the ceremonies used when approaching Mr. Kurtz,” I shouted. Such details would have been more intolerable than those heads drying on the stakes. After all, that was only a savage sight; while I seemed at one bound transported into some lightless region of subtle horrors where pure savagery was a relief, being something that had a right to exist in the sunshine. He looked at me with surprise; for him Kurtz was no idol of mine. He forgot I hadn’t heard those monologues on love, justice, conduct of life. If it had come to crawling, he crawled as much as the veriest savage. He said these were heads of rebels. I shocked him by laughing. Rebels! What would be next? Enemies, criminals, workers—and now rebels. Those rebellious heads looked very subdued to me on their sticks.

“You don’t know how such a life tries a man like Kurtz,” he cried.

“Well, and you?” I said.

“I! I! I am a simple man. I have no great thoughts. I want nothing from anybody. How can you compare me to—?” His feelings failed him. “I don’t understand,” he groaned. “I’ve been doing my best to keep him alive, and that’s enough. There hasn’t been a drop of medicine or a mouthful of invalid food for months. He was shamefully abandoned. A man like this—with such ideas. Shamefully! Shamefully! I—I—haven’t slept for the last ten nights—”

The long shadows of the forest had slipped downhill; beyond the symbolic row of stakes all was in gloom, while we yet stood in sunshine and the river abreast glittered still, with a murky and overshadowed bend above and below. Not a living soul was seen on the shore.

Suddenly round the corner of the house a group of men appeared, as though they had come up from the ground, bearing a stretcher in their midst. Instantly a cry arose whose shrillness pierced the still air; and, as if by enchantment, streams of human beings—with spears, with bows, with shields, with wild glances—poured into the clearing by the dark-faced and pensive forest. The bushes shook, the grass swayed, and then everything stood still in attentive immobility.

“Now, if he does not say the right thing to them we are all done for,” said the Russian. The knot with the stretcher stopped halfway as if petrified. The man on it sat up, lank, with an uplifted arm above the bearers’ shoulders. “Let us hope that the man who can talk so well of love in general will find some particular reason to spare us this time,” I said, resenting bitterly the absurd danger of being at the mercy of that atrocious phantom. I could not hear a sound, but through my glasses I saw the thin arm extended commandingly, the lower jaw moving, the eyes shining darkly in the bony head that nodded with grotesque jerks. Kurtz—Kurtz—that means short in German—don’t it? The name was as true as everything else in his life—and death. He looked at least seven feet long. His covering had fallen, and his body emerged from it pitiful and appalling as from a winding-sheet. I could see the cage of ribs astir, the bones of his arm waving; as though an animated image of death carved out of old ivory had been shaking its hand with menaces at a motionless crowd of bronze. He opened his mouth wide—it gave him a weirdly voracious aspect, as if he had wanted to swallow all the air, all the earth, all the men before him. A deep voice reached me faintly. He must have been shouting. He fell back suddenly; the bearers staggered forward, and almost at the same time the crowd vanished, without perceptible retreat, as if the forest had drawn them in again as the breath is drawn in a long aspiration.

Some of the pilgrims behind the stretcher carried his arms—two shot-guns, a heavy rifle, and a revolver-carbine—the thunderbolts of that pitiful Jupiter. The manager bent over him murmuring as he walked beside his head. They laid him down in one of the little cabins. His hand roamed feebly amongst torn envelopes and open letters littering the bed. I was struck by the fire of his eyes and the composed languor of his expression. It was not mere exhaustion. This shadow looked satiated and calm, as though for the moment it had had its fill of all the emotions.

He rustled one of the letters, looked straight at my face, and said, “I am glad.” Somebody had written to him about me. A voice! a voice! Grave, profound, vibrating—when the man did not seem capable of a whisper. However, he had enough strength in him—factitious, no doubt—to very nearly make an end of us, as you shall hear.

The manager appeared silently; I stepped out and he drew the curtain. The Russian, eyed curiously, was staring at the shore. Dark shapes could be made out flitting against the gloomy border; near the river two bronze figures under spotted skins stood warlike and still. And from right to left along the lighted shore moved a wild and gorgeous apparition of a woman.

She walked with measured steps, draped in striped and fringed cloths, treading the earth proudly, with a slight jingle and flash of barbarous ornaments—brass leggings to the knee, brass wire gauntlets to the elbow, a crimson spot on her cheek, innumerable necklaces of glass beads; bizarre things, charms, gifts of witch-men. She was savage and superb, wild-eyed and magnificent; ominous and stately in her deliberate progress. The immense wilderness seemed to look at her, pensive, as though at the image of its own tenebrous and passionate soul.

She came abreast, stood still, faced us. Her face had a tragic and fierce aspect of wild sorrow and dumb pain mingled with some struggling resolve. She looked at us, brooding over an inscrutable purpose. She made a step forward; there was a low jingle, a sway of fringed draperies; she stopped as if her heart had failed. She looked at us as if her life depended on the steadiness of her glance; suddenly she opened her bared arms and threw them up rigid above her head, as though to touch the sky, and at the same time the swift shadows darted out, gathering the steamer into a shadowy embrace. A formidable silence hung over the scene. She turned away slowly, passed into the bushes; once only her eyes gleamed back at us in the dusk.

“If she had offered to come aboard I really think I would have tried to shoot her,” said the man of patches, nervously. “I have been risking my life every day for the last fortnight to keep her out of the house. She got in one day and kicked up a row about those miserable rags I picked up to mend my clothes with. I wasn’t decent—must have been that—for she talked like a fury to Kurtz for an hour, pointing at me now and then. Luckily, I fancy Kurtz felt too ill to care, or there would have been mischief. I don’t understand.... Ah, well, it’s all over now.”

At this moment I heard Kurtz’s deep voice behind the curtain: “Save me!—save the ivory, you mean. Don’t tell me. Save me! Why, I’ve had to save you. You are interrupting my plans now. Sick! Sick! Not so sick as you would like to believe. Never mind. I’ll carry my ideas out yet—I will return. I’ll show you what can be done. You with your little peddling notions—you are interfering with me. I will return. I....”

The manager came out and took me aside. “He is very low, very low,” he said. “We have done all we could for him—haven’t we? But there is no disguising the fact, Mr. Kurtz has done more harm than good to the Company. He did not see the time was not ripe for vigorous action. Cautiously, cautiously—that’s my principle. The district is closed to us for a time. Deplorable! Upon the whole, the trade will suffer. I don’t deny there is a remarkable quantity of ivory—mostly fossil. We must save it, at all events—but look how precarious the position is—and why? Because the method is unsound.”

“Do you,” said I, looking at the shore, “call it ‘unsound method’?”

“Without doubt,” he exclaimed. “Don’t you?”

“No method at all,” I murmured.

“Exactly,” he exulted. “Shows a complete want of judgment. It is my duty to point it out in the proper quarter.”

“Oh,” said I, “that fellow—the brickmaker—will make a readable report for you.”

He seemed confounded. I turned mentally to Kurtz for relief. “Nevertheless I think Mr. Kurtz is a remarkable man,” I said with emphasis.

He started, dropped on me a heavy glance, said very quietly, “he was,” and turned his back. My hour of favour was over; I was lumped with Kurtz as a partisan of methods for which the time was not ripe. I was unsound! But it was something to have at least a choice of nightmares.

I had turned to the wilderness really, not to Mr. Kurtz, who, I was ready to admit, was as good as buried. For a moment I seemed to be buried in a vast grave full of unspeakable secrets—the smell of damp earth, victorious corruption, the darkness of an impenetrable night.... The Russian tapped my shoulder, mumbling of “brother seaman—knowledge of matters that would affect Mr. Kurtz’s reputation.”

“Well!” said I at last. “Speak out. As it happens, I am Mr. Kurtz’s friend—in a way.”

He stated with formality that had we not been of the same profession, he would have kept the matter to himself. “He suspected an active ill-will towards him on the part of these white men—”

“You are right,” I said, remembering a conversation. “The manager thinks you ought to be hanged.”

He showed concern. “I had better get out of the way quietly,” he said. “I can do no more for Kurtz now, and they would soon find some excuse. There’s a military post three hundred miles from here.”

“Perhaps you had better go if you have any friends amongst the savages near by.”

“Plenty,” he said. “They are simple people—and I want nothing, you know.” He bit his lip. “I don’t want any harm to happen to these whites here, but of course I was thinking of Mr. Kurtz’s reputation—but you are a brother seaman and—”

“All right,” said I. “Mr. Kurtz’s reputation is safe with me.”

He informed me, lowering his voice, that Kurtz had ordered the attack to be made on the steamer. “He hated sometimes the idea of being taken away—and then again.... He thought it would scare you away—that you would give it up, thinking him dead. I could not stop him. Oh, I had an awful time of it this last month.”

“Very well,” I said. “He is all right now.”

“Ye-e-es,” he muttered, not convinced. “But quiet—eh? It would be awful for his reputation if anybody here—”

I promised discretion. He had a canoe and three black fellows waiting. “Could you give me a few Martini-Henry cartridges?” I could, and did, with secrecy. He helped himself, with a wink, to a handful of my tobacco. “Between sailors—you know—good English tobacco.” At the pilot-house door he turned—“I say, haven’t you a pair of shoes you could spare?” He raised a leg. The soles were tied with knotted strings sandalwise. I found an old pair; he looked at them with admiration, tucked them under his arm. One pocket bulged with cartridges, from the other peeped a worn seamanship manual. He seemed to think himself excellently equipped for a renewed encounter with the wilderness. “Ah! I’ll never, never meet such a man again. You ought to have heard him recite poetry—his own, too. Poetry! Oh, he enlarged my mind!”

“Good-bye,” said I. He vanished in the night.

When I woke shortly after midnight his warning came to my mind with a hint of danger. On the hill a big fire burned; deep within the forest red gleams showed the exact position of the camp where Kurtz’s adorers kept uneasy vigil. The monotonous beating of a big drum filled the air with muffled shocks; a steady droning of many men chanting came like the humming of bees and had a narcotic effect upon my half-awake senses. I believe I dozed till an abrupt burst of yells woke me. It was cut short; the low droning went on with an effect of audible silence. I glanced into the cabin. A light was burning, but Mr. Kurtz was not there.

I was completely unnerved by a sheer blank fright, pure abstract terror; a moral shock, as if something monstrous and odious had been thrust upon me. Then the usual sense of commonplace danger, the possibility of an onslaught, was welcome and composing. There was an agent sleeping on deck within three feet of me. I left him to his slumbers and leaped ashore. I did not betray Mr. Kurtz—it was ordered I should never betray him. I was anxious to deal with this shadow by myself alone.

As soon as I got on the bank I saw a broad trail through the grass. “He can’t walk—he is crawling—I’ve got him,” I said to myself with exultation. The grass was wet with dew. I strode rapidly with clenched fists. I fancied I would fall upon him and give him a drubbing. Imbecile thoughts! The knitting old woman with the cat obtruded herself upon my memory; I saw a row of pilgrims squirting lead in the air. I imagined living alone and unarmed in the woods to an advanced age. Such silly things—you know. I confounded the drum with my heart and was pleased at its calm regularity.

I kept to the track—then stopped to listen. The night was very clear; a dark blue space sparkling with dew and starlight, in which black things stood very still. I thought I could see a kind of motion ahead. I was strangely cocksure. I left the track and ran in a wide semicircle (chuckling, I verily believe), to get in front of that stir—if indeed I had seen anything. I was circumventing Kurtz as though it had been a boyish game.

I came upon him; he got up in time. He rose, unsteady, long, pale, indistinct, like a vapour, and swayed slightly before me; behind me the fires loomed, and the murmur of many voices issued from the forest. I had cut him off cleverly; but when confronting him I seemed to come to my senses. Suppose he began to shout? Though he could hardly stand, there was vigour in his voice.

“Go away—hide yourself,” he said, in that profound tone. It was very awful. We were within thirty yards of the nearest fire. A black figure strode across the glow; it had horns—antelope horns—on its head. Some witch-man, fiendlike enough.

“Do you know what you are doing?” I whispered.

“Perfectly,” he answered, raising his voice for that single word; it sounded to me far off and yet loud, like a hail through a speaking-trumpet. “If he makes a row we are lost,” I thought. This was not a case for fisticuffs, even apart from my aversion to beat that Shadow. “You will be lost,” I said—“utterly lost.”

“I had immense plans,” he muttered irresolutely.

“Yes,” said I; “but if you try to shout I’ll smash your head with—” There was not a stick or a stone near. “I will throttle you for good,” I corrected.

“I was on the threshold of great things,” he pleaded, with a wistfulness that made my blood run cold. “And now for this stupid scoundrel—”

“Your success in Europe is assured in any case,” I affirmed steadily. I did not want the throttling of him; it would have been little use. I tried to break the spell—the heavy, mute spell of the wilderness—that drew him to its pitiless breast by awakening of brutal instincts, by the memory of gratified and monstrous passions. This alone, I was convinced, had driven him out to the bush, towards the gleam of fires, the throb of drums, the drone of incantations; this alone had beguiled his unlawful soul beyond bounds. The terror was not in being knocked on the head—which I was lively to; but in this, that I had to deal with a being to whom I could not appeal in the name of anything high or low. I had, even like the niggers, to invoke him—himself—his own exalted and incredible degradation. There was nothing either above or below him. He had kicked himself loose of the earth. Confound the man! he had kicked the very earth to pieces. He was alone, and I before him did not know whether I stood on the ground or floated in the air. We pronounced common everyday words—but they had behind them the suggestiveness of words heard in dreams. Soul! If anybody ever struggled with a soul, I am the man. And I wasn’t arguing with a lunatic either. His intelligence was perfectly clear—concentrated upon himself with horrible intensity, yet clear; therein was my only chance—barring the killing him then, which wasn’t so good on account of noise. But his soul was mad. Being alone, it had looked within itself, and, by heavens! it had gone mad. I had—for my sins—to look into it myself. No eloquence could have been so withering to one’s belief in mankind as his final burst of sincerity. He struggled with himself; I saw it—I heard it; the inconceivable mystery of a soul that knew no restraint, no faith, and no fear, yet struggling blindly with itself.

When I had him at last stretched on the couch, I wiped my forehead, while my legs shook as though I had carried half a ton down that hill. And yet I had only supported him, his bony arm clasped round my neck—he not much heavier than a child.

When next day we left at noon, the crowd behind the curtain of trees flowed out, filled the clearing, covered the slope with a mass of naked, breathing bronze. I steamed up a bit, then swung down stream; two thousand eyes followed the evolutions of the splashing, thumping, fierce river-demon beating the water and breathing black smoke. In front along the bank three men, plastered with bright red earth, strutted restlessly; when we came abreast they faced the river, stamped their feet, nodded their horned heads, swayed their scarlet bodies; they shook towards the river-demon a bunch of black feathers, a mangy skin, something like a dried gourd; they shouted strings of amazing words; and the deep murmurs of the crowd were like responses of some satanic litany.

We had carried Kurtz into the pilot-house; there was more air there. Lying on the couch, he stared through the open shutter. There was an eddy in the mass, and the woman with helmeted head and tawny cheeks rushed out to the very brink. She put out her hands, shouted, and all that wild mob took up the shout in a roaring chorus.

“Do you understand this?” I asked.

He kept looking out past me with fiery, longing eyes, with wistfulness and hate. He made no answer; a smile of indefinable meaning appeared on his colourless lips and a moment after twitched convulsively. “Do I not?” he said slowly, gasping, as if the words had been torn out of him.

I pulled the string of the whistle, because I saw the pilgrims getting out their rifles with an air of anticipating a jolly lark. At the screech there was a movement of abject terror through that wedged mass. “Don’t! don’t you frighten them away,” cried some one on deck disconsolately. I pulled the string time after time. They broke and ran, leaped, crouched, swerved; the three red chaps fell flat, face down, as though shot dead. Only the barbarous and superb woman did not so much as flinch, and stretched tragically her bare arms after us.

And then that imbecile crowd down on the deck started their little fun, and I could see nothing more for smoke.

The brown current ran swiftly out of the heart of darkness, bearing us towards the sea with twice the speed of our upward progress; and Kurtz’s life was running swiftly, too, ebbing out of his heart into the sea of inexorable time. The manager was placid; he had no vital anxieties now. The “affair” had come off as could be wished. I saw the time approaching when I would be left alone of the party of “unsound method.” The pilgrims looked upon me with disfavour. I was, so to speak, numbered with the dead. It is strange how I accepted this unforeseen partnership, this choice of nightmares.

Kurtz discoursed. A voice! a voice! It rang deep to the very last. It survived his strength to hide in the magnificent folds of eloquence the barren darkness of his heart. Oh, he struggled! The wastes of his weary brain were haunted by shadowy images now—images of wealth and fame revolving round his gift of noble and lofty expression. My Intended, my station, my career, my ideas—these were the subjects of elevated sentiments. The shade of the original Kurtz frequented the bedside of the hollow sham; both the diabolic love and the unearthly hate of the mysteries fought for the possession of that soul avid of lying fame, of sham distinction, of all the appearances of success and power.

Sometimes he was contemptibly childish. He desired to have kings meet him at railway-stations on his return from some ghastly Nowhere. “You show them you have in you something that is really profitable, and then there will be no limits to the recognition of your ability,” he would say. “Of course you must take care of the motives—right motives—always.”

The long reaches, monotonous bends, slipped past with their multitude of secular trees looking patiently after this grimy fragment of another world, the forerunner of change, of conquest, of trade, of massacres, of blessings. I looked ahead—piloting.

“Close the shutter,” said Kurtz suddenly; “I can’t bear to look at this.”

I did so.

There was a silence. “Oh, but I will wring your heart yet!” he cried at the invisible wilderness.

We broke down—as I had expected—and had to lie up for repairs at the head of an island. This delay shook Kurtz’s confidence. One morning he gave me a packet of papers and a photograph—the lot tied together with a shoe-string. “Keep this for me,” he said. “This noxious fool”—meaning the manager—“is capable of prying into my boxes when I am not looking.” In the afternoon I saw him lying with closed eyes; I withdrew, but I heard him mutter, “Live rightly, die, die...” He had been writing for the papers and meant to do so again, “for the furthering of my ideas. It’s a duty.”

His was an impenetrable darkness. I looked at him as you peer down at a man at the bottom of a precipice where the sun never shines. But I had no time for him; I was helping the engine-driver—taking to pieces leaky cylinders, straightening a bent connecting-rod, tending the little forge; toiling in a wretched scrap-heap—unless I had the shakes too bad to stand.

One evening coming in with a candle I was startled to hear him say, a little tremulously, “I am lying here in the dark waiting for death.” The light was within a foot of his eyes. I forced myself to murmur, “Oh, nonsense!” and stood over him as if transfixed.

Anything approaching the change that came over his features I have never seen before. It was as though a veil had been rent. I saw on that ivory face sombre pride, ruthless power, craven terror—intense and hopeless despair. Did he live his life again in every detail during that supreme moment of complete knowledge? He cried in a whisper at some image, some vision—he cried out twice, a cry that was no more than a breath:

“The horror! The horror!”

I blew the candle out and left the cabin. The pilgrims were dining; I took my place opposite the manager, who lifted his eyes with a questioning glance. He leaned back, serene, with that peculiar smile sealing the unexpressed depths of his meanness. A continuous shower of small flies streamed upon the lamp, upon the cloth, upon our hands and faces. Suddenly the manager’s boy put his insolent black head in the doorway, and said in a tone of scathing contempt:

“Mistah Kurtz—he dead.”

All the pilgrims rushed out. I remained and went on with my dinner. I believe I was considered brutally callous. However, I did not eat much. There was a lamp—light, don’t you know—and outside it was so beastly, beastly dark. I went no more near the remarkable man who had pronounced a judgment upon the adventures of his soul. The voice was gone. What else had been there? But I am aware that next day the pilgrims buried something in a muddy hole.

And then they very nearly buried me.

However, I did not go to join Kurtz there and then. I remained to dream the nightmare out to the end, and to show my loyalty to Kurtz once more. Destiny. Droll thing life is—that mysterious arrangement of merciless logic for a futile purpose. The most you can hope from it is some knowledge of yourself—that comes too late. I have wrestled with death. It takes place in an impalpable greyness, without spectators, without clamour, without glory, without much belief in your own right, and still less in that of your adversary. I was within a hair’s breadth of the last opportunity for pronouncement, and I found with humiliation that probably I would have nothing to say. This is the reason why I affirm that Kurtz was a remarkable man. He had something to say. He said it. Since I had peeped over the edge myself, I understand better the meaning of his stare, that could not see the flame of the candle, but was wide enough to embrace the universe. He had summed up—he had judged. “The horror!” He was a remarkable man. After all, this was the expression of some sort of belief; it had candour, conviction, a vibrating note of revolt; it had the appalling face of a glimpsed truth—the strange commingling of desire and hate. No, it is not my own extremity I remember best. It is his extremity that I seem to have lived through. True, he had made that last stride, stepped over the edge, while I drew back my hesitating foot. Perhaps all wisdom, and all truth, and all sincerity, are compressed into that inappreciable moment in which we step over the threshold of the invisible. Perhaps! Better his cry—much better. It was an affirmation, a moral victory paid for by innumerable defeats, by abominable terrors and satisfactions. But it was a victory! That is why I have remained loyal to Kurtz to the last, and even beyond, when a long time after I heard once more, not his own voice, but the echo of his magnificent eloquence thrown to me from a soul as translucently pure as a cliff of crystal.

No, they did not bury me, though there is a period I remember mistily, like a passage through some inconceivable world that had no hope in it and no desire. I found myself back in the sepulchral city resenting the sight of people hurrying through the streets to filch a little money, to devour their infamous cookery, to gulp their unwholesome beer, to dream insignificant dreams. They trespassed upon my thoughts, intruders whose knowledge of life was to me an irritating pretence. Their bearing, simply the bearing of commonplace individuals going about their business in the assurance of perfect safety, was offensive to me like the outrageous flauntings of folly in the face of a danger it cannot comprehend. I tottered about the streets—there were various affairs to settle—grinning bitterly at respectable persons. My dear aunt’s endeavours to nurse up my strength seemed beside the mark. It was not my strength that wanted nursing, it was my imagination.

I kept the bundle of papers given me by Kurtz, not knowing exactly what to do with it. His mother had died lately, watched over, as I was told, by his Intended. A clean-shaved man, with an official manner and gold-rimmed spectacles, called one day and made inquiries, suavely pressing, about what he denominated certain “documents.” I had had two rows with the manager on the subject out there; I had refused to give up the smallest scrap; I took the same attitude with the spectacled man. He became darkly menacing, argued that the Company had the right to every bit of information about its “territories.” He invoked the name of science. I offered him the report on the “Suppression of Savage Customs,” with the postscriptum torn off. He sniffed at it. “This is not what we had a right to expect,” he remarked. “Expect nothing else,” I said. “There are only private letters.” He withdrew upon some threat of legal proceedings; another fellow, calling himself Kurtz’s cousin, appeared: an organist, I believe. He was anxious to hear all the details about his dear relative’s last moments, and incidentally gave me to understand that Kurtz had been essentially a great musician. I had no reason to doubt him; to this day I am unable to say what was Kurtz’s profession; whether he ever had any—which was the greatest of his talents. Ultimately a journalist anxious to know something of the fate of his “dear colleague” turned up. He informed me Kurtz’s proper sphere ought to have been politics “on the popular side.” “He really couldn’t write a bit,” he confessed—“but heavens! how that man could talk. He had faith—don’t you see?—he had the faith. He could get himself to believe anything—anything. He would have been a splendid leader of an extreme party.”

“What party?” I asked.

“Any party,” answered the other. “He was an—an—extremist.”

He asked with a flash of curiosity what had induced him to go out there. “Yes,” said I, and handed him the famous Report for publication, if he thought fit. He judged “it would do,” and took himself off.

Thus I was left at last with a slim packet of letters and the girl’s portrait. She struck me as beautiful—I mean she had a beautiful expression. One felt that no manipulation of light and pose could have conveyed the delicate shade of truthfulness upon those features. She seemed ready to listen without reservation, without suspicion, without a thought for herself. I concluded I would go and give her back her portrait and those letters myself. Curiosity? Yes; and also some other feeling perhaps. All that had been Kurtz’s had passed out of my hands: his soul, his body, his station, his plans, his ivory, his career. There remained only his memory and his Intended—and I wanted to give that up, too, to the past.

I thought his memory like the other memories of the dead that accumulate in every man’s life; but before the high and ponderous door, between the tall houses of a street as still as a well-kept alley in a cemetery, I had a vision of him on the stretcher, opening his mouth voraciously, as if to devour all the earth with all its mankind. He lived then before me; he lived as much as he had ever lived—a shadow insatiable of splendid appearances, of frightful realities; a shadow darker than the night, and draped nobly in the folds of a gorgeous eloquence. The vision seemed to enter the house with me—the stretcher, the phantom-bearers, the obedient worshippers, the gloom of the forests, the glitter of the reach, the beat of the drum, regular and muffled like the beating of a heart—the heart of a conquering darkness. It was a moment of triumph for the wilderness, an invading and vengeful rush which I must keep back alone for the salvation of another soul. The memory of what I had heard him say there, within the patient woods, those broken phrases came back in their ominous simplicity. I remembered his abject pleading, his abject threats, the colossal scale of his vile desires, the torment, the tempestuous anguish of his soul. And later I seemed to see his collected languid manner, when he said one day, “This lot of ivory now is really mine. The Company did not pay for it. I collected it myself at a very great personal risk. I am afraid they will try to claim it as theirs though. H’m. It is a difficult case. What do you think I ought to do—resist? Eh? I want no more than justice.”

He wanted no more than justice. I rang the bell before a mahogany door, and while I waited he seemed to stare at me out of the glassy panel—stare with that wide and immense stare embracing, condemning, loathing all the universe. I seemed to hear the whispered cry, “The horror! The horror!”

The dusk was falling. I had to wait in a lofty drawing-room with three long windows like luminous and bedraped columns. A grand piano stood massively in a corner; with dark gleams on the flat surfaces like a sombre sarcophagus. A high door opened—closed. I rose.

She came forward, all in black, with a pale head, floating towards me in the dusk. She was in mourning. It was more than a year since his death; she seemed as though she would mourn forever. She took both my hands in hers and murmured, “I had heard you were coming.” She had a mature capacity for fidelity, for belief, for suffering. The room seemed darker, as if the sad light of the evening had taken refuge on her forehead. This fair hair, this pale visage, this pure brow, seemed surrounded by an ashy halo from which dark eyes looked out—guileless, profound, confident, trustful. She carried her sorrowful head as though proud of that sorrow, as though to say, “I—I alone know how to mourn for him as he deserves.” But while we were still shaking hands, such a look of desolation came upon her face that I perceived she was one of those creatures that are not the playthings of Time. For her he had died only yesterday. And the impression was so powerful that for me, too, he seemed to have died only yesterday—nay, this very minute. I saw her and him in the same instant—his death and her sorrow. She had said, with a deep catch of the breath, “I have survived,” while my strained ears seemed to hear distinctly the summing-up whisper of his eternal condemnation.

She motioned me to a chair. We sat. I laid the packet gently on the little table, and she put her hand over it.

“You knew him well,” she murmured.

“Intimacy grows quickly out there,” I said. “I knew him as well as it is possible for one man to know another.”

“And you admired him,” she said. “It was impossible to know him and not to admire him. Was it?”

“He was a remarkable man,” I said, unsteadily. Then before the appealing fixity of her gaze I went on, “It was impossible not to—”

“Love him,” she finished eagerly, silencing me. “How true! how true! But when you think that no one knew him so well as I! I had all his noble confidence. I knew him best.”

“You knew him best,” I repeated. And perhaps she did. But with every word the room was growing darker, and only her forehead, smooth and white, remained illumined by the inextinguishable light of belief and love.

“You were his friend,” she went on. “His friend,” she repeated, a little louder. “You must have been, if he had given you this, and sent you to me. I feel I can speak to you—and oh! I must speak. I want you—you who have heard his last words—to know I have been worthy of him.... It is not pride.... Yes! I am proud to know I understood him better than any one on earth—he told me so himself. And since his mother died I have had no one—no one—to—to—”

I listened. The darkness deepened. The girl talked, easing her pain in the certitude of my sympathy; she talked as thirsty men drink. I had heard that her engagement had been disapproved by her people. He wasn’t rich enough or something. And indeed I don’t know whether he had not been a pauper all his life. He had given me some reason to infer that impatience of comparative poverty drove him out there.

“... Who was not his friend who had heard him speak once?” she was saying. “He drew men towards him by what was best in them.” She looked at me with intensity. “It is the gift of the great,” she went on, and the sound of her low voice seemed to have the accompaniment of all the other sounds, full of mystery, desolation, and sorrow, I had ever heard—the ripple of the river, the soughing of trees, the murmurs of crowds, the faint ring of incomprehensible words cried from afar, the whisper of a voice speaking from beyond the threshold of an eternal darkness. “But you have heard him! You know!” she cried.

“Yes, I know,” I said with something like despair in my heart, but bowing my head before the faith that was in her, before that great and saving illusion that shone with an unearthly glow in the darkness, in the triumphant darkness from which I could not have defended her—from which I could not even defend myself.

“What a loss to me—to us!”—she corrected herself; then added in a murmur, “To the world.” By the last gleams of twilight I could see the glitter of her eyes, full of tears—of tears that would not fall.

“I have been very happy—very fortunate—very proud,” she went on. “Too fortunate. Too happy for a little while. And now I am unhappy for—for life.”

She stood up; her fair hair seemed to catch all the remaining light. I rose, too.

“And of all this,” she went on mournfully, “of all his promise, and of all his greatness, of his generous mind, of his noble heart, nothing remains—nothing but a memory. You and I—”

“We shall always remember him,” I said hastily.

“No!” she cried. “It is impossible that all this should be lost—that such a life should be sacrificed to leave nothing—but sorrow. You know what vast plans he had. I knew of them, too—I could not perhaps understand—but others knew of them. Something must remain. His words, at least, have not died.”

“His words will remain,” I said.

“And his example,” she whispered to herself. “Men looked up to him—his goodness shone in every act. His example—”

“True,” I said; “his example, too. Yes, his example. I forgot that.”

“But I do not. I cannot—I cannot believe—not yet. I cannot believe that I shall never see him again, that nobody will see him again, never, never, never.”

She put out her arms as if after a retreating figure, stretching them back with clasped pale hands across the fading sheen of the window. Never see him! I saw him clearly enough then. I shall see this eloquent phantom as long as I live, and I shall see her, too, a tragic Shade, resembling in this gesture another one, tragic also, and bedecked with powerless charms, stretching bare brown arms over the glitter of the infernal stream, the stream of darkness. She said suddenly very low, “He died as he lived.”

“His end,” said I, with dull anger stirring in me, “was in every way worthy of his life.”

“And I was not with him,” she murmured. My anger subsided before infinite pity.

“Everything that could be done—” I mumbled.

“Ah, but I believed in him more than any one on earth—more than his own mother, more than—himself. He needed me! Me! I would have treasured every sigh, every word, every sign, every glance.”

I felt a chill grip on my chest. “Don’t,” I said, in a muffled voice.

“Forgive me. I—I have mourned so long in silence—in silence.... You were with him—to the last? I think of his loneliness. Nobody near to understand him as I would have understood. Perhaps no one to hear....”

“To the very end,” I said, shakily. “I heard his very last words....” I stopped in a fright.

“Repeat them,” she murmured in a heart-broken tone. “I want—I want—something—something—to—to live with.”

I was on the point of crying at her, “Don’t you hear them?” The dusk was repeating them in a persistent whisper all around us, swelling like the first of a rising wind. “The horror! The horror!”

“His last word—to live with,” she insisted. “Don’t you understand I loved him—I loved him—I loved him!”

I pulled myself together and spoke slowly.

“The last word he pronounced was—your name.”

I heard a light sigh and then my heart stood still, stopped by an exulting and terrible cry, the cry of inconceivable triumph and of unspeakable pain. “I knew it—I was sure!”... She knew. She was sure. I heard her weeping; she had hidden her face. It seemed to me that the house would collapse, that the heavens would fall. But nothing happened. The heavens do not fall for such a trifle. Would they have fallen if I had rendered Kurtz that justice which was his due? Hadn’t he said he wanted only justice? But I couldn’t. I could not tell her. It would have been too dark—too dark altogether.

Marlow ceased, and sat apart, indistinct and silent, in the pose of a meditating Buddha. Nobody moved for a time.

“We have lost the first of the ebb,” said the captain suddenly. I raised my head. The offing was barred by a black bank of clouds, and the tranquil waterway leading to the uttermost ends of the earth flowed sombre under an overcast sky—seemed to lead into the heart of an immense darkness.
